entries.cc5ad26e5c7ee91e784a71bb48ff71b45071a8d5: <div sID="gen5603" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="1Sam.17" sID="1Sam.17"/> <div eID="gen5603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5604" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5605" type="x-p"/> David is the man whom God now delights to honour, for he is a man after his own heart. We read in the foregoing chapter how, after he was anointed, Providence made him famous in the court; we read in this chapter how Providence made him much more famous in the camp, and, by both, not only marked him for a great man, but fitted him for the throne for which he was designed. In the court he was only Saul's physician; but in the camp Israel's champion; there he fairly fought, and beat Goliath of Gath. In the story observe, I. What a noble figure Goliath made, and how daringly he challenged the armies of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1-1Sam.17.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. What a mean figure David made, when Providence brought him to the army, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12-1Sam.17.30">ver. 12-30</reference>. III. The unparalleled bravery wherewith David undertook to encounter this Philistine, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.31-1Sam.17.39">ver. 31-39</reference>. IV. The pious resolution with which he attacked him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.40-1Sam.17.47">ver. 40-47</reference>. V. The glorious victory he obtained over him with a sling and a stone, and the advantage which the Israelites thereby gained against the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.48-1Sam.17.54">ver. 48-54</reference>. VI. The great notice which was hereupon taken of David at court, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.55-1Sam.17.58">ver. 55-58</reference>.
entries.7422f27d7db991dd074e5fccb3447ba93c1c79ea: <div eID="gen5605" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5604" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Goliath's Challenge to Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1060.)</title> <div sID="gen5606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which <hi type="italic">belongeth</hi> to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Saul and the men of Israel were gathered together, and pitched by the valley of Elah, and set the battle in array against the Philistines. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the Philistines stood on a mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on a mountain on the other side: and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a valley between them. <hi type="super">4</hi> And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height <hi type="italic">was</hi> six cubits and a span. <hi type="super">5</hi> And <hi type="italic">he had</hi> a helmet of brass upon his head, and he <hi type="italic">was</hi> armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat <hi type="italic">was</hi> five thousand shekels of brass. <hi type="super">6</hi> And <hi type="italic">he had</hi> greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the staff of his spear <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a weaver's beam; and his spear's head <hi type="italic">weighed</hi> six hundred shekels of iron: and one bearing a shield went before him. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he stood and cried unto the armies of Israel, and said unto them, Why are ye come out to set <hi type="italic">your</hi> battle in array? <hi type="italic">am</hi> not I a Philistine, and ye servants to Saul? choose you a man for you, and let him come down to me. <hi type="super">9</hi> If he be able to fight with me, and to kill me, then will we be your servants: but if I prevail against him, and kill him, then shall ye be our servants, and serve us. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the Philistine said, I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together. <hi type="super">11</hi> When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid. <div eID="gen5606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5607" type="x-p"/> It was not long ago that the Philistines were soundly beaten, and put to the worse, before Israel, and they would have been totally routed if Saul's rashness had not prevented; but here we have them making head again. Observe, <div eID="gen5607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5608" type="x-p"/> I. How they <hi type="italic">defied Israel with their armies,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1">v. 1</reference>. They made a descent upon the Israelites' country, and possessed themselves, as it should seem, of some part of it, for they encamped in a place <hi type="italic">which belonged to Judah.</hi> Israel's ground would never have been footing for Philistine-armies if Israel had been faithful to their God. The Philistines (it is probable) had heard that Samuel had fallen out with Saul and forsaken him, and no longer assisted and advised him, and that Saul had grown melancholy and unfit for business, and this news encouraged them to make this attempt for the retrieving of the credit they had lately lost. The enemies of the church are watchful to take all advantages, and they never have greater advantages than when her protectors have provoked God's Spirit and prophets to leave them. Saul mustered his forces, and faced them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.2-1Sam.17.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. And here we must take notice, 1. That the evil spirit, for the present, had left Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.23">ch. xvi. 23</reference>. David's harp having given him some relief, perhaps the alarms and affairs of the war prevented the return of the distemper. Business is a good antidote against melancholy. Let the mind have something without to fasten on and employ itself about, and it will be the less in danger of preying upon itself. God, in mercy to Israel, suspended the judgment for a while; for how distracted must the affairs of the public have been if at this juncture the prince had been distracted! 2. That David for the present had returned to Bethlehem, and had left the court, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.15">v. 15</reference>. When Saul had no further occasion to use him for the relief of his distemper, though, being anointed, he had a very good private reason, and, having a grant of the place of Saul's armour-bearer, he had a very plausible pretence to have continued his attendance, as a retainer to the court, yet he went home to Bethlehem, and returned to keep his father's sheep; this was a rare instance, in a young man that stood so fair for preferment, of humility and affection to his parents. He knew better than most do how to come down again after he had begun to rise, and strangely preferred the retirements of the pastoral life before all the pleasures and gaieties of the court. None more fit for honour than he, nor that deserved it better, and yet none more dead to it. <div eID="gen5608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5609" type="x-p"/> II. How they defied Israel with their champion Goliath, whom they were almost as proud of as he was of himself, hoping by him to recover their reputation and dominion. Perhaps the army of the Israelites was superior in number and strength to that of the Philistines, which made the Philistines decline a battle, and stand at bay with them, desiring rather to put the issue upon a single combat, in which, having such a champion, they hoped to gain the victory. Now concerning this champion observe, <div eID="gen5609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5610" type="x-p"/> 1. His prodigious size. He was of the sons of Anak, who at Gath kept their ground in Joshua's time (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.22">Josh. xi. 22</reference>), and kept up a race of giants there, of which Goliath was one, and, it is probable, one of the largest. He was in height <hi type="italic">six cubits and a span,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.4">v. 4</reference>. The learned bishop Cumberland has made it out that the scripture-cubit was above twenty-one inches (above three inches more than our half-yard) and a span was half a cubit, by which computation Goliath wanted but eight inches of four yard in height, eleven feet and four inches, a monstrous stature, and which made him very formidable, especially if he had strength and spirit proportionable. <div eID="gen5610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5611" type="x-p"/> 2. His armour. Art, as well as nature, made him terrible. He was well furnished with defensive armour (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.5-1Sam.17.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">A helmet of brass on his head, a coat of mail,</hi> made of brass plates laid over one another, like the scales of a fish; and, because his legs would lie most within the reach of an ordinary man, he wore brass boots, and had a large corselet of brass about his neck. The coat is said to weigh 5000 shekels, and a shekel was half an ounce avoirdupois, a vast weight for a man to carry, all the other parts of his armour being proportionable. But some think it should be translated, not the <hi type="italic">weight</hi> of the coat, but the <hi type="italic">value</hi> of it, was 5000 shekels; so much it cost. His offensive weapons were extraordinary, of which his spear only is here described, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.7">v. 7</reference>. It was like a weaver's beam. His arm could manage that which an ordinary man could scarcely heave. His shield only, which was the lightest of all his accoutrements, was carried before him by his esquire, probably for state; for he that was clad in brass little needed a shield. <div eID="gen5611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5612" type="x-p"/> 3. His challenge. The Philistines having chosen him for their champion, to save themselves from the hazard of battle, he here throws down the gauntlet, and bids defiance to the armies of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.8-1Sam.17.10">v. 8-10</reference>. He came into the valley that lay between the camps, and, his voice probably being as much stronger than other people's as his arm was, he cried so as to make them all hear him, <hi type="italic">Give me a man, that we may fight together.</hi> He looked upon himself with admiration, because he was so much taller and stronger than all about him; his heart (says bishop Hall) nothing but a lump of proud flesh. He looked upon Israel with disdain, because they had none among them of such a monstrous bulk, and defies them to find a man among them bold enough to enter the list with him. (1.) He upbraids them with their folly in drawing an army together: "<hi type="italic">Why have you come to set the battle in array?</hi> How dare you oppose the mighty Philistines?" Or, "Why should the two armies engage, when the controversy may be sooner decided, with only the expense of one life and the hazard of another?" (2.) He offers to put the war entirely upon the issue of the duel he proposes: "If your champion kill me, we will be your servants; if I kill him, you shall be ours." This, says bishop Patrick, was only a bravado, for no nation would be willing thus to venture its all upon the success of one man, nor is it justifiable; notwithstanding Goliath's stipulation here, when he was killed the Philistines did not stand to his word, nor submit themselves as servants to Israel. When he boasts, <hi type="italic">I am a Philistine, and you are servants to Saul,</hi> he would have it thought a great piece of condescension in him, who was a chief ruler, to enter the lists with an Israelite; for he looked on them as no better than slaves. The Chaldee paraphrase brings him in boasting that he was the man that had killed Hophni and Phinehas and taken the ark prisoner, but that the Philistines had never given him so much as the command of a regiment in recompence of his services, whereas Saul had been made king for his services: "Let him therefore take up the challenge." <div eID="gen5612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5613" type="x-p"/> 4. The terror this struck upon Israel: <hi type="italic">Saul and his army were greatly afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.11">v. 11</reference>. The people would not have been dismayed but that they observed Saul's courage failed him; and it is not to be expected that, if the leader be a coward, the followers should be bold. We found before, when the Spirit of the Lord came upon Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.6">ch. xi. 6</reference>), none could be more daring nor forward to answer the challenge of Nahash the Ammonite, but now that the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord had departed from him</hi> even the big looks and big words of a single Philistine make him change colour. But where was Jonathan all this while? Why did not he accept the challenge, who, in the last war, had so bravely engaged a whole army of Philistines? Doubtless he did not feel himself stirred up of God to it, as he did in the former case. As the best, so the bravest men, are no more than what God makes them. Jonathan must now sit still, because the honour of engaging Goliath is reserved for David. In great and good actions, the wind of the Spirit blows when and where he listeth. Now the pious Israelites lament their king's breach with Samuel.
entries.bec143ece8a7ed875728bba7e35adaaeb321254f: <div eID="gen5613" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Comes to the Camp of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1060.)</title> <div sID="gen5614" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Now David <hi type="italic">was</hi> the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem-judah, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Jesse; and he had eight sons: and the man went among men <hi type="italic">for</hi> an old man in the days of Saul. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the three eldest sons of Jesse went <hi type="italic">and</hi> followed Saul to the battle: and the names of his three sons that went to the battle <hi type="italic">were</hi> Eliab the firstborn, and next unto him Abinadab, and the third Shammah. <hi type="super">14</hi> And David <hi type="italic">was</hi> the youngest: and the three eldest followed Saul. <hi type="super">15</hi> But David went and returned from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the Philistine drew near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Jesse said unto David his son, Take now for thy brethren an ephah of this parched <hi type="italic">corn,</hi> and these ten loaves, and run to the camp to thy brethren; <hi type="super">18</hi> And carry these ten cheeses unto the captain of <hi type="italic">their</hi> thousand, and look how thy brethren fare, and take their pledge. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now Saul, and they, and all the men of Israel, <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines. <hi type="super">20</hi> And David rose up early in the morning, and left the sheep with a keeper, and took, and went, as Jesse had commanded him; and he came to the trench, as the host was going forth to the fight, and shouted for the battle. <hi type="super">21</hi> For Israel and the Philistines had put the battle in array, army against army. <hi type="super">22</hi> And David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper of the carriage, and ran into the army, and came and saluted his brethren. <hi type="super">23</hi> And as he talked with them, behold, there came up the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, out of the armies of the Philistines, and spake according to the same words: and David heard <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> And all the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him, and were sore afraid. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the men of Israel said, Have ye seen this man that is come up? surely to defy Israel is he come up: and it shall be, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel. <hi type="super">26</hi> And David spake to the men that stood by him, saying, What shall be done to the man that killeth this Philistine, and taketh away the reproach from Israel? for who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God? <hi type="super">27</hi> And the people answered him after this manner, saying, So shall it be done to the man that killeth him. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle. <hi type="super">29</hi> And David said, What have I now done? <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> not a cause? <hi type="super">30</hi> And he turned from him toward another, and spake after the same manner: and the people answered him again after the former manner. <div eID="gen5614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5615" type="x-p"/> Forty days the two armies lay encamped facing one another, each advantageously posted, but neither forward to engage. Either they were parleying and treating of an accommodation or they were waiting for recruits; and perhaps there were frequent skirmishes between small detached parties. All this while, twice a day, morning and evening, did the insulting champion appear in the field and repeat his challenge, his own heart growing more and more proud for his not being answered and the people of Israel more and more timorous, while God designed hereby to ripen him for destruction and to make Israel's deliverance the more illustrious. All this while David is keeping his father's sheep, but at the end of forty days Providence brings him to the field to win and wear the laurel which no other Israelite dares venture for. We have in these verses, <div eID="gen5615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5616" type="x-p"/> I. The present state of his family. His father was old (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He went among men for an old man,</hi> was taken notice of for his great age, above what was usual at that time, and therefore was excused from pubic services, and went not in person to the wars, but sent his sons; he had the honours paid him that were due his age, his hoary head was a crown of glory to him. David's three elder brethren, who perhaps envied his place at the court, got their father to send for him home, and let them go to the camp, where they hoped to signalize themselves and eclipse him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.13-1Sam.17.14">v. 13, 14</reference>), while David himself was so far from being proud of the services he had done his prince, or ambitious of further preferment, that he not only returned from court to the obscurity of his father's house, but to care, and toil, and (as it proved, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34">v. 34</reference>) the peril, of <hi type="italic">keeping his father's sheep.</hi> It was the praise of this humility that it came after he had the honour of a courtier, and the reward of it that it came before the honour of a conqueror. <hi type="italic">Before honour is humility.</hi> Now he had that opportunity of mediation and prayer, and other acts of devotion, which fitted him for what he was destined to more than all the military exercises of that inglorious camp could do. <div eID="gen5616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5617" type="x-p"/> II. The orders his father gave him to go and visit his brethren in the camp. He did not himself ask leave to go, to satisfy his curiosity, or to gain experience and make observations; but his father sent him on a mean and homely errand, on which any of his servants might have gone. He must carry some bread and cheese to his brethren, ten loaves with some parched corn for themselves (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.17">v. 17</reference>) and ten cheeses (which, it seems, he thought too good for them) for a present to their colonel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.18">v. 18</reference>. David must still be the drudge of the family, though he was to be the greatest ornament of it. He had not so much as an ass at command to carry his load, but must take it on his back, and yet run to the camp. Jesse, we thought, was privy to his being anointed, and yet industriously kept him thus mean and obscure, probably to hide him from the eye of suspicion and envy, knowing that he was anointed to a crown in reversion. He must observe how his brethren fared, whether they were not reduced to short allowance, now that the encampment continued so long, that, if need were, he might send them more provisions. And he must take their pledge, that is, if they had pawned any thing, he must redeem it; <hi type="italic">take notice of their company,</hi> so some observe, whom they associate with, and what sort of life they lead. Perhaps David, like Joseph, had formerly brought to his father their evil report, and now he sends him to enquire concerning their manners. See the care the pious parents about their children when they are abroad from them, especially in places of temptation; they are solicitous how they conduct themselves, and particularly what company they keep. Let children think of this, and conduct themselves accordingly, remembering that, when they are from under their parents' eye, they are still under God's eye. <div eID="gen5617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5618" type="x-p"/> III. David's dutiful obedience to his father's command. His prudence and care made him be up early (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.20">v. 20</reference>), and yet not to leave his sheep without a keeper, so faithful was he in a few things and therefore the fitter to be made ruler over many things, and so well had he learnt to obey before he pretended to command. God's providence brought him to the camp very seasonably, when both sides had set the battle in array, and, as it should seem, were more likely to come to an engagement than they had yet been during all the forty days, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.21">v. 21</reference>. Both sides were now preparing to fight. Jesse little thought of sending his son to the army just at that critical juncture, but the wise God orders the time and all the circumstances of actions and affairs so as to serve his designs of securing the interests of Israel and advancing the men after his own heart. Now observe here, <div eID="gen5618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5619" type="x-p"/> 1. How brisk and lively David was, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.22">v. 22</reference>. What articles he brought he honestly took care of, and left them with those that had the charge of the bag and baggage; but, though he had come a long journey with a great load, he <hi type="italic">ran into the army,</hi> to see what was doing there, and to pay his respects to his brethren. <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man</hi> thus <hi type="italic">diligent in his business,</hi> he is in the way of preferment, <hi type="italic">he shall stand before kings.</hi> <div eID="gen5619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5620" type="x-p"/> 2. How bold and daring the Philistine was, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.23">v. 23</reference>. Now that the armies were drawn out into a line of battle he appeared first to renew his challenge, vainly imagining that he was in the eager chase of his own glory and triumph, whereas really he was but courting his own destruction. <div eID="gen5620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5621" type="x-p"/> 3. How timorous and faint-hearted the men of Israel were. Though they had, for forty days together, been used to his haughty looks and threatening language, and, having seen no execution done by either, might have learned to despise both, yet, upon his approach, they <hi type="italic">fled from him and were greatly afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.24">v. 24</reference>. One Philistine could never thus have chased 1000 Israelites, and put 10,000 to flight, unless their Rock, being treacherously forsaken by them, had justly <hi type="italic">sold them, and shut them up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deut. xxxii. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen5621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5622" type="x-p"/> 4. How high Saul bid for a champion. Though he was the tallest of all the men of Israel, and, if he had not been so, while he kept close to God might himself have safely taken up the gauntlet which this insolent Philistine threw down, yet, the Spirit of the Lord having departed from him, he durst not do it, nor press Jonathan to do it; but whoever will do it shall have as good preferment as he can give him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">v. 25</reference>. If the hope of wealth and honour will prevail with any man to expose himself so far, it is proclaimed that the bold adventurer, if he come off, shall marry the king's daughter and have a good portion with her; but, as it should seem, whether he come off or no, his <hi type="italic">father's house shall be free in Israel,</hi> from all toll, tribute, custom, and services to the crown, or shall be ennobled and advanced to the peerage. <div eID="gen5622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5623" type="x-p"/> 5. How much concerned David was to assert the honour of God and Israel against the impudent challenges of this champion. He asked what reward was promised to him that should slay this Philistine (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.26">v. 26</reference>), though he knew already, not because he was ambitious of the honour, but because he would have it taken notice of, and reported to Saul, how much he resented the indignity hereby done to Israel and Israel's God. He might have presumed so far upon his acquaintance and interest at court as to go himself to Saul to offer his service; but his modesty would not let him do this. It was one of his own rules, before it was one of his son's proverbs, <hi type="italic">Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.6">Prov. xxv. 6</reference>); yet his zeal put him upon that method which he hoped would bring him into this great engagement. Two considerations, it seems, fired David with a holy indignation:— (1.) That the challenger was one that was uncircumcised, a stranger to God and out of covenant with him. (2.) That the challenged were the armies of the living God, devoted to him, employed by him and for him, so that the affronts offered to them reflected upon the living God himself, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he could not bear. When therefore some had told him what was the reward proposed for killing the Philistine (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.27">v. 27</reference>) he asked others (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.30">v. 30</reference>), with the same resentment, which he expected would at length come to Saul's ear. <div eID="gen5623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5624" type="x-p"/> 6. How he was brow-beaten and discouraged by his eldest brother Eliab, who, taking notice of his forwardness, fell into a passion upon it, and gave David very abusive language, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.28">v. 28</reference>. Consider this, (1.) As the fruit of Eliab's jealousy. He was the eldest brother, and David the youngest, and perhaps it had been customary with him (as it is with too many elder brothers) to trample upon him and take every occasion to chide him. But those who thus exalt themselves over their juniors may perhaps live to see themselves, by a righteous providence, abased, and those to whom they are abusive exalted. Time may come when the elder may serve the younger. But Eliab was now vexed that his younger brother should speak those bold words against the Philistine which he himself durst not say. He knew what honour David had already had in the court, and, if he should now get honour in the camp (from which he thought he had found means effectually to seclude him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.15">v. 15</reference>), the glory of his elder brethren would be eclipsed and stained; and therefore (such is the nature of jealousy) he would rather that Goliath should triumph over Israel than that David should be the man that should triumph over him. <hi type="italic">Wrath is cruel and anger is outrageous, but who can stand before envy,</hi> especially the envy of a brother, the keenness of which Jacob, and Joseph, and David experienced? See <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Prov. xviii. 19</reference>. It is very ill-favoured language that Eliab here gives him; not only unjust and unkind, but, at this time, basely ungrateful; for David was now sent by his father, as Joseph by his, on a kind of visit to his brethren. Eliab intended, in what he said, not only to grieve and discourage David himself, and quench that noble fire which he perceived glowing in his breast, but to represent him to those about him as an idle proud lad, not fit to be taken notice of. He gives them to understand that his business was only to keep sheep, and falsely insinuates that he was a careless unfaithful shepherd; though he had left his charge in good hands (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.20">v. 20</reference>), yet he must tauntingly be asked, <hi type="italic">With whom hast thou left those few sheep?</hi> Though he came down now to the camp in obedience to his father and kindness to his brethren, and Eliab knew this, yet his coming is turned to his reproach: "Thou hast come down, not to do any service, but to gratify thy own curiosity, and only to look about thee;" and thence he will infer <hi type="italic">the pride and naughtiness of his heart,</hi> and pretends to know it as certainly as if he were in his bosom. David could appeal to God concerning his humility and sincerity (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Ps. xvii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.131.1">cxxxi. 1</reference>) and at this time gave proofs of both, and yet could not escape this hard character from his own brother. See the folly, absurdity, and wickedness, of a proud and envious passion; how groundless its jealousies are, how unjust its censures, how unfair its representations, how bitter its invectives, and how indecent its language. God, by his grace, keep us from such a spirit! (2.) As a trial of David's meekness, patience and constancy. A short trial it was, and he approved himself well in it; for, [1.] He bore the provocation with admirable temper (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What have I now done?</hi> What fault have I committed, for which I should thus be chidden? <hi type="italic">Is there not a cause</hi> for my coming to the camp, when my father sent me? <hi type="italic">Is there not a cause</hi> for my resenting the injury done to Israel's honour by Goliath's challenges?" He had right and reason on his side, and knew it, and therefore did not render railing for railing, but with a soft answer turned away his brother's wrath. This conquest of his own passion was in some respects more honourable than his conquest of Goliath. <hi type="italic">He that hath rule over his own spirit is better than the mighty.</hi> It was no time for David to quarrel with his brother when the Philistines were upon them. The more threatening the church's enemies are the more forbearing her friends should be with one another. [2.] He broke through the discouragement with admirable resolution. He would not be driven off from his thoughts of engaging the Philistine by the ill-will of his brother. Those that undertake great and public services must not think it strange if they be discountenanced and opposed by those from whom they had reason to expect support and assistance; but must humbly go on with their work, in the face not only of their enemies' threats, but of their friends' slights and suspicions.
entries.ff02b9344bf85c3df288603ab2e0c25283149346: <div eID="gen5624" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Meets Goliath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1060.)</title> <div sID="gen5625" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And when the words were heard which David spake, they rehearsed <hi type="italic">them</hi> before Saul: and he sent for him. <hi type="super">32</hi> And David said to Saul, Let no man's heart fail because of him; thy servant will go and fight with this Philistine. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Saul said to David, Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou <hi type="italic">art but</hi> a youth, and he a man of war from his youth. <hi type="super">34</hi> And David said unto Saul, Thy servant kept his father's sheep, and there came a lion, and a bear, and took a lamb out of the flock: <hi type="super">35</hi> And I went out after him, and smote him, and delivered <hi type="italic">it</hi> out of his mouth: and when he arose against me, I caught <hi type="italic">him</hi> by his beard, and smote him, and slew him. <hi type="super">36</hi> Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God. <hi type="super">37</hi> David said moreover, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be with thee. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Saul armed David with his armour, and he put a helmet of brass upon his head; also he armed him with a coat of mail. <hi type="super">39</hi> And David girded his sword upon his armour, and he assayed to go; for he had not proved <hi type="italic">it.</hi> And David said unto Saul, I cannot go with these; for I have not proved <hi type="italic">them.</hi> And David put them off him. <div eID="gen5625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5626" type="x-p"/> David is at length presented to Saul for his champion (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.31">v. 31</reference>) and he bravely undertakes to fight the Philistine (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let no man's heart fail because of him.</hi> It would have reflected too much upon the valour of his prince if he had said, <hi type="italic">Let not thy heart fail;</hi> therefore he speaks generally: <hi type="italic">Let no man's heart fail.</hi> A little shepherd, come but this morning from keeping sheep, has more courage than all the mighty men of Israel, and encourages them. Thus does God often send good words to his Israel, and do great things for them, by the weak and foolish things of the world. David only desires a commission from Saul to go and fight with the Philistine, but says nothing to him of the reward he had proposed, because that was not the thing he was ambitious of, but only the honour of serving God and his country: nor would he seem to question Saul's generosity. Two things David had to do with Saul:— <div eID="gen5626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5627" type="x-p"/> I. To get clear of the objection Saul made against his undertaking. "Alas!" says Saul, "thou hast a good heart to it, but art by no means an equal match for this Philistine. To engage with him is to throw away a life which may better be reserved for more agreeable services. <hi type="italic">Thou art but a youth,</hi> rash and inconsiderate, weak and unversed in arms: he is a man that has the head and hands of a man, <hi type="italic">a man of war,</hi> trained up and inured to it <hi type="italic">from his youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.33">v. 33</reference>), and how canst thou expect but that he will be too hard for thee?" David, as he had answered his brother's passion with meekness, so he answered Saul's fear with faith, and <hi type="italic">gives a reason of the hope</hi> which was in him that he should conquer the Philistine, to the satisfaction of Saul. We have reason to fear that Saul had no great acquaintance with nor regard to the word of God, and therefore David, in reasoning with him, fetched not his arguments and encouragements thence, how much soever he had an eye to it in his own mind. But he argues from experience; though he was but a youth, and never in the wars, yet perhaps he had done as much as the killing of Goliath came to, for he had had, by divine assistance, spirit enough to encounter and strength enough to subdue a lion once and another time a bear that robbed him of his lambs, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.36">v. 34-36</reference>. To these he compares this uncircumcised Philistine, looks upon him to be as much a ravenous beast as either of them, and therefore doubts not but to deal as easily with him; and hereby he gives Saul to understand that he was not so inexperienced in hazardous combats as he took him to be. <div eID="gen5627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5628" type="x-p"/> 1. He tells his story like a man of spirit. He is not ashamed to own that he kept his father's sheep, which his brother had just now upbraided him with. So far is he from concealing it that from his employment as a shepherd he fetches the experience that now animated him. But he lets those about him know that he was no ordinary shepherd. Whatever our profession or calling is, be it ever so mean, we should labour to excel in it, and do the business of it in the best manner. When David kept sheep, (1.) He approved himself very careful and tender of his flock, though it was not his own, but his father's. He could not see a lamb in distress but he would venture his life to rescue it. This temper made him fit to be a king, to whom the lives of subjects should be dear and their blood precious (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Ps. lxxii. 14</reference>), and fit to be a type of Christ, the good Shepherd, who <hi type="italic">gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them in his bosom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa. xl. 11</reference>), and who not only ventured, but <hi type="italic">laid down his life for his sheep.</hi> Thus too was David fit to be an example to ministers with the utmost care and diligence to watch for souls, that they be not a prey to the roaring lion. (2.) He approved himself very bold and brave in the defence of his flock. This was that which he was now concerned to give proof of, and better evidence could not be demanded than this: "Thy servant not only rescued the lambs, but, to revenge the injury, <hi type="italic">slew both the lion and the bear.</hi>" <div eID="gen5628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5629" type="x-p"/> 2. He applies his story like a man of faith. He owns (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.37">v. 37</reference>) it was <hi type="italic">the Lord that delivered him from the lion and the bear;</hi> to him he gives the praise of that great achievement, and thence he infers, <hi type="italic">He will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.</hi> "The lion and the bear were enemies only to me and my sheep, and it was in defence of my own interest that I attacked them; but this Philistine is an enemy to God and Israel, <hi type="italic">defies the armies of the living God,</hi> and it is for their honour that I attack him." Note, (1.) Our experiences ought to be improved by us as our encouragements to trust in God and venture in the way of duty. He that has delivered does and will. (2.) By the care which common Providence takes of the inferior creatures, and the protection they are under, we may be encouraged to depend upon that special Providence which surrounds the Israel of God. He that sets bounds to the waves of the sea and the rage of wild beasts can and will restrain the wrath of wicked men. Paul seems to allude to this of David (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17-2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 17, 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion,</hi> and therefore, I trust, <hi type="italic">the Lord shall deliver me.</hi> And perhaps David here thought of the story of Samson, and encouraged himself with it; for his slaying a lion was a happy presage of his many illustrious victories over the Philistines in single combat. Thus David took off Saul's objection against his undertaking, and gained a commission to fight the Philistine, with which Saul gave him a hearty good wish; since he would not venture himself, he prayed for him that would: <hi type="italic">Go, and the Lord be with thee,</hi> a good word, if it was not spoken customarily, and in a formal manner, as too often it is. But David has somewhat to do likewise, <div eID="gen5629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5630" type="x-p"/> II. To get clear of the armour wherewith Saul would, by all means, have him dressed up when he went upon this great action (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">He armed David with his armour,</hi> not that which he wore himself, the disproportion of his stature would not admit that, but some that he kept in his armoury, little thinking that he on whom he now put his helmet and coat of mail must shortly inherit his crown and robe. David, being not yet resolved which way to attack his enemy, <hi type="italic">girded on his sword,</hi> not knowing, as yet, but he should have occasion to make use of it; but he found the armour would but encumber him, and would be rather his burden than his defence, and therefore he desires leave of Saul to put them off again: <hi type="italic">I cannot go with these, for I have not proved them,</hi> that is, "I have never been accustomed to such accoutrements as these." We may suppose Saul's armour was both very fine and very firm, but what good would it do David if it were not fit, or if he knew not how to manage himself in it? Those that aim at things above their education and usage, and covet the attire and armour of princes, forget that that is the best for us which we are fit for and accustomed to; if we had our desire, we should wish to be in our own coat again, and should say, "We cannot go with these;" we had therefore better go without them.
entries.83cb88f88f97c9693c918a0fd3e69c043d8dfa27: <div eID="gen5630" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Kills Goliath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1060.)</title> <div sID="gen5631" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">40</hi> And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling <hi type="italic">was</hi> in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine. <hi type="super">41</hi> And the Philistine came on and drew near unto David; and the man that bare the shield <hi type="italic">went</hi> before him. <hi type="super">42</hi> And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was <hi type="italic">but</hi> a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance. <hi type="super">43</hi> And the Philistine said unto David, <hi type="italic">Am</hi> I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves? And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. <hi type="super">44</hi> And the Philistine said to David, Come to me, and I will give thy flesh unto the fowls of the air, and to the beasts of the field. <hi type="super">45</hi> Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied. <hi type="super">46</hi> This day will the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. <hi type="super">47</hi> And all this assembly shall know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's, and he will give you into our hands. <div eID="gen5631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5632" type="x-p"/> We are now coming near this famous combat, and have in these verses the preparations and remonstrances made on both sides. <div eID="gen5632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5633" type="x-p"/> I. The preparations made on both sides for the encounter. The Philistine was already fixed, as he had been daily for the last forty days. Well might he go with his armour, for he had sufficiently proved it. Only we are told (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.41">v. 41</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">came on and drew near,</hi> a signal, it is likely, being given that his challenge was accepted, and, as if he distrusted his helmet and coat of mail, a man went before him, <hi type="italic">carrying his shield,</hi> for his own hands were full with his sword and spear, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.45">v. 45</reference>. But what arms and ammunition is David furnished with? Truly none but what he brought with him as a shepherd; no breastplate, nor corselet, but his plain shepherd's coat; no spear, but his staff; no sword nor bow, but his sling; no quiver, but his scrip; nor any arrows, but, instead of them, five smooth stones picked up out of the brook, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.40">v. 40</reference>. By this it appeared that his confidence was purely in the power of God, and not in any sufficiency of his own, and that now at length he who put it into his heart to fight the Philistine put it into his head with what weapons to do it. <div eID="gen5633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5634" type="x-p"/> II. The conference which precedes the encounter, in which observe, <div eID="gen5634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5635" type="x-p"/> 1. How very proud Goliath was, (1.) With what scorn he looked upon his adversary, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.42">v. 42</reference>. He looked about, expecting to meet some tall strong man, but, when he saw what a mean figure he made with whom he was to engage, he disdained him, thought it below him to enter the lists with him, fearing that the contemptibleness of the champion he contended with would lessen the glory of his victory. He took notice of his person, that he was but a youth, not come to his strength, <hi type="italic">ruddy and of a fair countenance,</hi> fitter to accompany the virgins of Israel in their dances (if mixed dancing was then in use) than to lead on the men of Israel in their battles. He took notice of his array with great indignation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.43">v. 43</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?</hi> Dost thou think to beat me as easily as thou dost thy shepherd's dog?" (2.) With what confidence he presumed upon his success. He cursed David by his gods, imprecating the impotent vengeance of his idols against him, thinking these fire-balls thrown about him would secure his success: and therefore, in confidence of that, he darts his grimaces, as if threatening words would kill (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.44">v. 44</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come to me, and I will give thy flesh to the fowls of the air,</hi> it will be a tender and delicate feast for them." Thus the security and presumption of fools destroy them. <div eID="gen5635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5636" type="x-p"/> 2. How very pious David was. His speech savours nothing of ostentation, but God is all in all in it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.45-1Sam.17.47">v. 45-47</reference>. (1.) He derives his authority from God: "<hi type="italic">I come to thee</hi> by warrant and commission from heaven, <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord,</hi> who has called me to and anointed me for this undertaking, who, by his universal providence, is the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> of all hosts, and therefore has power to do what he pleases, and, by the special grace of his covenant, is <hi type="italic">the God of the armies of Israel,</hi> and therefore has engaged and will employ his power for their protection, and against thee who hast impiously defied them." The name of God David relied on, as Goliath did on his sword and spear. See <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.10-Ps.118.11">cxviii. 10, 11</reference>. (2.) He depends for success upon God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.46">v. 46</reference>. David speaks with as much assurance as Goliath had done, but upon better ground; it is his faith that says, "<hi type="italic">This day will the Lord deliver thee into my hand,</hi> and not only thy carcase, but the carcases of the host of the Philistines, shall be given to the birds and beasts of prey." (3.) He devotes the praise and glory of all to God. He did not, like Goliath, seek his own honour, but the honour of God, not doubting but by the success of this action, [1.] All the world should be made to know that there is a God, and that the God of Israel is the one only living and true God, and all other pretended deities are vanity and a lie. [2.] All Israel (whom he calls not this army, but <hi type="italic">this assembly,</hi> or church, because they were now religiously attending the <hi type="italic">goings of their God and King,</hi> as they used to do <hi type="italic">in the sanctuary</hi>) shall <hi type="italic">know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">v. 47</reference>), but can, when he pleases, save without either and against both, <reference osisRef="Ps.46.9">Ps. xlvi. 9</reference>. David addresses himself to this combat rather as a priest that was going to offer a sacrifice to the justice of God than as a soldier that was going to engage an enemy of his country.
entries.f15ce7d17a093c9a06d8bc9dc44eb236bbaa585c: <div eID="gen5636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5637" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">48</hi> And it came to pass, when the Philistine arose, and came and drew nigh to meet David, that David hasted, and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine. <hi type="super">49</hi> And David put his hand in his bag, and took thence a stone, and slang <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth. <hi type="super">50</hi> So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no sword in the hand of David. <hi type="super">51</hi> Therefore David ran, and stood upon the Philistine, and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof, and slew him, and cut off his head therewith. And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled. <hi type="super">52</hi> And the men of Israel and of Judah arose, and shouted, and pursued the Philistines, until thou come to the valley, and to the gates of Ekron. And the wounded of the Philistines fell down by the way to Shaaraim, even unto Gath, and unto Ekron. <hi type="super">53</hi> And the children of Israel returned from chasing after the Philistines, and they spoiled their tents. <hi type="super">54</hi> And David took the head of the Philistine, and brought it to Jerusalem; but he put his armour in his tent. <hi type="super">55</hi> And when Saul saw David go forth against the Philistine, he said unto Abner, the captain of the host, Abner, whose son <hi type="italic">is</hi> this youth? And Abner said, <hi type="italic">As</hi> thy soul liveth, O king, I cannot tell. <hi type="super">56</hi> And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling <hi type="italic">is.</hi> <hi type="super">57</hi> And as David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, Abner took him, and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand. <hi type="super">58</hi> And Saul said to him, Whose son <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> young man? And David answered, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the son of thy servant Jesse the Bethlehemite. <div eID="gen5637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5638" type="x-p"/> Here is 1. The engagement between the two champions, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.48">v. 48</reference>. To this engagement the Philistine advanced with a great deal of state and gravity; if he must encounter a pigmy, yet it shall be with the magnificence of a giant and a grandee. This is intimated in the manner of expression: He <hi type="italic">arose, and came, and drew nigh,</hi> like a stalking mountain, overlaid with brass and iron, <hi type="italic">to meet David.</hi> David advanced with no less activity and cheerfulness, as one that aimed more to do execution than to make a figure: He <hi type="italic">hasted, and ran,</hi> being lightly clad, to <hi type="italic">meet the Philistine.</hi> We may imagine with what tenderness and compassion the Israelites saw such a pleasing youth as this throwing himself into the mouth of destruction, but he knew whom he had believed and for whom he acted. 2. The fall of Goliath in this engagement. He was in no haste, because in no fear, but confident that he should soon at one stroke cleave his adversary's head; but, while he was preparing to do it solemnly, David did his business effectually, without any parade: he slang a stone which hit him in the forehead, and, in the twinkling of an eye, fetched him to the ground, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.49">v. 49</reference>. Goliath knew there were famous slingers in Israel (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">Judg. xx. 16</reference>), yet was either so forgetful or presumptuous as to go with the beaver of his helmet open, and thither, to the only part left exposed, not so much David's art as God's providence directed the stone, and brought it with such force that it sunk into his head, notwithstanding the impudence with which his forehead was brazened. See how frail and uncertain life is, even when it thinks itself best fortified, and how quickly, how easily, and with how small a matter, the passage may be opened for life to go out and death to enter. Goliath himself <hi type="italic">has not power over the spirit to retain the spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Eccl. viii. 8</reference>. Let not the strong man glory in his strength, nor the armed man in his armour. See how God resists the proud and pours contempt upon those that bid defiance to him and his people. None ever hardened his heart against God and prospered. One of the Rabbin thinks that when Goliath said to David, <hi type="italic">Come, and I will give thy flesh to the fowls of the air,</hi> he threw up his head so hastily that his helmet fell off, and so left his broad forehead a fair mark for David. To complete the execution, David drew Goliath's own sword, a two-handed weapon for David, and with it <hi type="italic">cut off his head,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.51">v. 51</reference>. What need had David to take a sword of his own? his enemy's sword shall serve his purpose, when he has occasion for one. God is greatly glorified when his proud enemies are cut off with their own sword and he makes <hi type="italic">their own tongues to fall upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. David's victory over Goliath was typical of the triumphs of the son of David over Satan and all the powers of darkness, whom he <hi type="italic">spoiled, and made a show of them openly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>), and we through him are <hi type="italic">more than conquerors.</hi> 3. The defeat of the Philistines' army hereupon. They relied wholly upon the strength of their champion, and therefore, when they saw him slain, they did not, as Goliath had offered, throw down their arms and surrender themselves servants to Israel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.9">v. 9</reference>), but took to their heels, being wholly dispirited, and thinking it to no purpose to oppose one before whom such a mighty man had fallen: <hi type="italic">They fled</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.51">v. 51</reference>), and this put life into the Israelites, who <hi type="italic">shouted and pursued them</hi> (David, it is probable, leading them on in the pursuit) even to the gates of their own cities, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.52">v. 52</reference>. In their return from the chase they seized all the baggage, plundered the tents (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.53">v. 53</reference>), and enriched themselves with the spoil. 4. David's disposal of his trophies, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.54">v. 54</reference>. He brought the head of the Philistine to Jerusalem, to be a terror to the Jebusites, who held the strong-hold of Sion: it is probable that he carried it in triumph to other cities. <hi type="italic">His armour he laid up in his tent;</hi> only the sword was preserved behind the ephod in the tabernacle, as consecrated to God, and a memorial of the victory to his honour, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">ch. xxi. 9</reference>. 5. The notice that was taken of David. Though he had been at court formerly, yet, having been for some time absent (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.15">v. 15</reference>), Saul had forgotten him, being melancholy and mindless, and little thinking that his musician would have spirit enough to be his champion; and therefore, as if he had never seen him before, he asked whose son he was. Abner was a stranger to him, but brought him to Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.57">v. 57</reference>), and he gave a modest account of himself, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.58">v. 58</reference>. And now he was introduced to the court with much greater advantages than before, in which he owned God's hand performing all things for him.  <chapter eID="1Sam.17"/> <div eID="gen5638" type="x-p"/>

entries.9d1456bcfd296b7c36acb92e03cb43947d0364d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2666"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <div sID="gen3617" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1-1Sam.17.3">1Sa 17:1-3</reference>. The Israelites and Philistines Being Ready to Battle.<div eID="gen3617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2666"/><hi type="bold">1. the Philistines gathered together their armies--</hi>twenty-seven years after their overthrow at Michmash. Having now recovered their spirits and strength, they sought an opportunity of wiping out the infamy of that national disaster, as well as to regain their lost ascendency over Israel.<div eID="gen3618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shocoh--</hi>now Shuweikeh, a town in the western plains of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>), nine Roman miles from Eleutheropolis, toward Jerusalem [Robinson].<div eID="gen3619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Azekah--</hi>a small place in the neighborhood.<div eID="gen3620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ephes-dammim--</hi>or, "Pas-dammim" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference>), "the portion" or "effusion of blood," situated between the other two. <div eID="gen3621" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bc977f767b4b39822c5979c2829fa89f5f92162: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2667"/><div sID="gen3622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2667"/><hi type="bold">2. valley of Elah--</hi>that is, "the Terebinth," now Wady Er-Sumt [Robinson]. Another valley somewhat to the north, now called Wady Beit Hanina, has been fixed on by the tradition of ages.<div eID="gen3622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3623" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.4-1Sam.17.11">1Sa 17:4-11</reference>. Goliath Challenges a Combat. <div eID="gen3623" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa8d247fc16f600f7cf5760488653d59f01292f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2668"/><div sID="gen3624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2668"/><hi type="bold">4-11. a champion--</hi>Hebrew, a "man between two"; that is, a person who, on the part of his own people, undertook to determine the national quarrel by engaging in single combat with a chosen warrior in the hostile army. <div eID="gen3624" type="x-p"/>
entries.c776178c1ee4f151c96a0f6fee3e5fbd4d3faf05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2673"/><div sID="gen3633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2673"/><hi type="bold">17. Take now for thy brethren an ephah of this parched corn, and these ten loaves--</hi>In those times campaigns seldom lasted above a few days at a time. The soldiers were volunteers or militia, who were supplied with provisions from time to time by their friends at home. <div eID="gen3633" type="x-p"/>
entries.878013133e30356ec18408a7ff5b9b7d0adbcf8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2674"/><div sID="gen3634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2674"/><hi type="bold">18. carry these ten cheeses to the captain--</hi>to enlist his kind attention. Oriental cheeses are very small; and although they are frequently made of so soft a consistence as to resemble curds, those which David carried seem to have been fully formed, pressed, and sufficiently dried to admit of their being carried.<div eID="gen3634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take their pledge--</hi>Tokens of the soldiers' health and safety were sent home in the convenient form of a lock of their hair, or piece of their nail, or such like. <div eID="gen3635" type="x-p"/>
entries.57a73e090c8115cca7217504985c2f23f9eec507: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2675"/><div sID="gen3636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2675"/><hi type="bold">20. David left the sheep with a keeper--</hi>This is the only instance in which the hired shepherd is distinguished from the master or one of his family.<div eID="gen3636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trench--</hi>some feeble attempt at a rampart. It appears (see Margin) to have been formed by a line of carts or chariots, which, from the earliest times, was the practice of nomad people. <div eID="gen3637" type="x-p"/>
entries.34bb269a872b08a43616e233896a975e58f714fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2676"/><div sID="gen3638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2676"/><hi type="bold">22. left his carriage in the hand of the keeper of the carriage--</hi>to make his way to the standard of Judah. <div eID="gen3638" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a5c7774d557df79d896b2e1b9b9c1fd1ae4af4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2677"/><div sID="gen3639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2677"/><hi type="bold">25. make his father's house free in Israel--</hi>His family should be exempted from the impositions and services to which the general body of the Israelites were subjected. <div eID="gen3639" type="x-p"/>
entries.c093dc94e8637d0b71f68cd17171efa474459734: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2678"/><div sID="gen3640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2678"/><hi type="bold">34-36. a lion, and a bear--</hi>There were two different rencontres, for those animals prowl alone. The bear must have been a Syrian bear, which is believed to be a distinct species, or perhaps a variety, of the brown bear. The beard applies to the lion alone. Those feats seem to have been performed with no weapons more effective than the rude staves and stones of the field, or his shepherd's crook. <div eID="gen3640" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef5cfcd5a68ecd3ae9a6e3d207f5c1dcdb8f2e8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2679"/><div sID="gen3641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2679"/><hi type="bold">37. The Lord that delivered me--</hi>It would have been natural for a youth, and especially an Oriental youth, to make a parade of his gallantry. But David's piety sank all consideration of his own prowess and ascribed the success of those achievements to the divine aid, which he felt assured would not be withheld from him in a cause which so intimately concerned the safety and honor of His people.<div eID="gen3641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Saul said unto David, Go, and the Lord be with thee--</hi>The pious language of the modest but valiant youth impressed the monarch's heart. He felt that it indicated the true military confidence for Israel, and, therefore, made up his mind, without any demur, to sanction a combat on which the fate of his kingdom depended, and with a champion supporting his interests apparently so unequal to the task. <div eID="gen3642" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0def9807c25b54e8eb02d12d9fbfd35948eedb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2680"/><div sID="gen3643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2680"/><hi type="bold">38-39. Saul armed David with his armour--</hi>The ancient Hebrews were particularly attentive to the personal safety of their warriors, and hence Saul equipped the youthful champion with his own defensive accoutrements, which would be of the best style. It is probable that Saul's coat of mail, or corslet, was a loose shirt, otherwise it could not have fitted both a stripling and a man of the colossal stature of the king. <div eID="gen3643" type="x-p"/>
entries.74f6e4772eef432f76036978f69292f16a9a22f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2681"/><div sID="gen3644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2681"/><hi type="bold">40. brook--</hi>wady.<div eID="gen3644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bag--</hi>or scrip for containing his daily food.<div eID="gen3645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sling--</hi>The sling consisted of a double rope with a thong, probably of leather, to receive the stone. The slinger held a second stone in his left hand. David chose five stones, as a reserve, in case the first should fail. Shepherds in the East carry a sling and stones still, for the purpose of driving away, or killing, the enemies that prowl about the flock. <div eID="gen3646" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c9fff59980b77370a38de7030d5c2d9f97d3c9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2682"/><div sID="gen3647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2682"/><hi type="bold">42-47. the Philistine said ... said David to the Philistine--</hi>When the two champions met, they generally made each of them a speech, and sometimes recited some verses, filled with allusions and epithets of the most opprobrious kind, hurling contempt and defiance at one another. This kind of abusive dialogue is common among the Arab combatants still. David's speech, however, presents a striking contrast to the usual strain of these invectives. It was full of pious trust, and to God he ascribed all the glory of the triumph he anticipated. <div eID="gen3647" type="x-p"/>
entries.54b1ac2abd4b8bc700dbd0055559054b495f369f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2683"/><div sID="gen3648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2683"/><hi type="bold">49. smote the Philistine in his forehead--</hi>At the opening for the eyes--that was the only exposed part of his body. <div eID="gen3648" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e152df20e369aaaef2a57b3ecd967a6db94ea7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2684"/><div sID="gen3649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2684"/><hi type="bold">51. cut off his head--</hi>not as an evidence of the giant's death, for his slaughter had been effected in presence of the whole army, but as a trophy to be borne to Saul. The heads of slain enemies are always regarded in the East as the most welcome tokens of victory. <div eID="gen3649" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bca066d9c78257c032476f8b1b48b493fd8dab7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2685"/><div sID="gen3650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2685"/><hi type="bold">52. Shaaraim--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Josh.15.36">Jos 15:36</reference>). <div eID="gen3650" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfbcc25889a0ccbfdf43c107f900688382b61619: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2686"/><div sID="gen3651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2686"/><hi type="bold">54. tent--</hi>the sacred tabernacle. David dedicated the sword of Goliath as a votive offering to the Lord. <div eID="gen3651" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dc3d99fceb3df3d27ff7d6051feedc35569cd57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2687"/><div sID="gen3652" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2687"/><hi type="bold">55-58. Saul ... said unto Abner ... whose son is this youth?--</hi>A young man is more spoken of in many Eastern countries by his father's name than his own. The growth of the beard, and other changes on a now full-grown youth, prevented the king from recognizing his former favorite minstrel [1Sa 16:23]. <chapter eID="1Sam.17"/>

entries.7c5f14c4a503b1be7ee67b9461d65aa1eb055c52: <div eID="gen10150" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10151" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10152" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10152" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10151" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10153" type="x-p"/> The Philistines gather together against Israel at Ephes-dammim, and Saul and his men pitch their camp near the valley of Elah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1-1Sam.17.3">1Sam 17:1-3</reference>. Goliath of Gath, a gigantic man, whose height was six cubits and a span, defies the armies of Israel, and proposes to end all contests by single combat; his armor is described, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.4-1Sam.17.11">1Sam 17:4-11</reference>. Saul and his host are greatly dismayed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12">1Sam 17:12</reference>. David, having been sent by his father with provisions to his brethren in the army, hears the challenge, inquires into the circumstances, thinks it a reproach to Israel that no man can be found to accept the challenge, is brought before Saul, and proposes to undertake the combat, vv. 13-32. Saul objects to his youth and inexperience, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.33">1Sam 17:33</reference>. David shows the grounds on which he undertakes it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.37">1Sam 17:34-37</reference>. Saul arms him with his own armor: but David, finding them an encumbrance, puts them off, and takes his staff, his sling, and five stones out of the brook, and goes to meet Goliath, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.38-1Sam.17.40">1Sam 17:38-40</reference>. The Philistine draws near, despises, defies, and curses him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.41-1Sam.17.44">1Sam 17:41-44</reference>. David retorts his defiance, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.45-1Sam.17.47">1Sam 17:45-47</reference>. They draw near to each other, and David slings a stone, hits Goliath in the forehead, slays him, and cuts off his head with his own sword, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.48-1Sam.17.51">1Sam 17:48-51</reference>. The Philistines flee, and are pursued by the Israelites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.52">1Sam 17:52</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.53">1Sam 17:53</reference>. David brings the head of the Philistine to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.54">1Sam 17:54</reference>. Conversation between Saul and Abner concerning David, who is in consequence brought before Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.55-1Sam.17.58">1Sam 17:55-58</reference>. <div eID="gen10153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10154" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10155" type="x-p"/> Now the Philistines gathered together - Calmet thinks that this war happened eight years after the anointing of David, and ten or twelve years after the war with the Amalekites. We have already seen that there was war between Saul and the Philistines all his days. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.52">1Sam 14:52</reference>. <div eID="gen10155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10156" type="x-p"/> Shochoh and Azekah - Places which lay to the south of Jerusalem and to the west of Bethlehem; about five leagues from the former. Ephes-dammim was somewhere in the vicinity, but it is not known where. See Calmet.
entries.450b8d52a215e3ba610ea4dc83a47225ac677392: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10157" type="x-p"/> The valley of Elah - Some translate this the turpentine valley, or the valley of the terebinth trees; and others, the valley of oaks. The situation of this valley is well known.
entries.c94959b0653cfb7f8899c6cd5b926357607feb4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10158" type="x-p"/> The Philistines stood on a mountain - These were two eminences or hills, from which they could see and talk with each other.
entries.30bd0971117bd5091b8fd4aa403aa9e3d65be5af: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10159" type="x-p"/> There went out a champion - Our word champion comes from campus, the field; Campio est enim ille qui pugnat in campo, hoc est, in castris, "Champion is he, properly, who fights in the field; i.e., in camps." A man well skilled in arms, strong, brave, and patriotic. <div eID="gen10159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10160" type="x-p"/> But is this the meaning of the original איש הבנים ish habbenayim, a middle man, the man between two; that is, as here, the man who undertakes to settle the disputes between two armies or nations. So our ancient champions settled disputes between contending parties by what was termed camp fight, hence the campio or champion. The versions know not well what to make of this man. The Vulgate calls him sir spurius, "a bastard;" the Septuagint, ανηρ δυνατος, "a strong or powerful man;" the Targum, גברא מביניהון gabra mibbeyneyhon, "a man from between them;" the Arabic, rujil jibar, "a great or gigantic man;" the Syriac is the same; and Josephus terms him ανηρ παμμεγεθιστατος, "an immensely great man." The Vulgate has given him the notation of spurius or bastard, because it considered the original as expressing a son of two, i.e., a man whose parents are unknown. Among all these I consider our word champion, as explained above, the best and most appropriate to the original terms. <div eID="gen10160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10161" type="x-p"/> Whose height was six cubits and a span - The word cubit signifies the length from cubitus, the elbow, to the top of the middle finger, which is generally rated at one foot six inches. The span is the distance from the top of the middle finger to the end of the thumb, when extended as far as they can stretch on a plain; this is ordinarily nine inches. Were we sure that these were the measures, and their extent, which are intended in the original words, we could easily ascertain the height of this Philistine; it would then be nine feet nine inches, which is a tremendous height for a man. <div eID="gen10161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10162" type="x-p"/> But the versions are not all agreed in his height. The Septuagint read τεσσαρων πηχεων και σπιθαμης, four cubits and a span; and Josephus reads the same. It is necessary however to observe that the Septuagint, in the Codex Alexandrinus, read with the Hebrew text. But what was the length of the ancient cubit? This has been variously computed; eighteen inches, twenty inches and a half, and twenty-one inches. If we take the first measurement, he was nine feet nine; if the second, and read palm instead of span, with the Vulgate and others, he was ten feet seven inches and a half; if we take the last, which is the estimate of Graevius, with the span, he was eleven feet three inches; or if we go to the exactest measurement, as laid down in Bishop Cumberland's tables, where he computes the cubit at 21.888 inches, the span at 10.944 inches, and the palm at 3.684 inches, then the six cubits and the span will make exactly 11 feet 10.272 inches. If we take the palm instead of the span, then the height will be 11 feet 3.012 inches. But I still think that the nine feet nine inches is the most reasonable.
entries.07470ec59d66efac93cf10b2c4b606f34f2ac4b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10163" type="x-p"/> He was armed with a coat of mail - The words in the original, שרון קשקשים shiryon kaskassim, mean a coat of mail formed of plates of brass overlapping each other, like the scales of a fish, or tiles of a house. This is the true notion of the original terms. <div eID="gen10163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10164" type="x-p"/> With thin plates of brass or iron, overlapping each other, were the ancient coats of mail formed in different countries; many formed in this way may be now seen in the tower of London. <div eID="gen10164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10165" type="x-p"/> The weight - five thousand shekels - Following Bishop Cumberland's tables, and rating the shekel at two hundred and nineteen grains, and the Roman ounce at four hundred and thirty-eight grains, we find that Goliath's coat of mail, weighing five thousand shekels, was exactly one hundred and fifty-six pounds four ounces avoirdupois. A vast weight for a coat of mail, but not all out of proportion to the man.
entries.4bbc1f39268902e9ddaf97de05ae0dc4cf25f794: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10166" type="x-p"/> Greaves of brass upon his legs - This species of armor may be seen on many ancient monuments. It was a plate of brass (though perhaps sometimes formed of laminae or plates, like the mail) which covered the shin or fore part of the leg, from the knee down to the instep, and was buckled with straps behind the leg. From ancient monuments we find that it was commonly worn only on one leg. Vegetius, de Re Militari, says, Pedites Scutati etiam ferreas ocreas in dextris cruribus copebantur accipere. "The foot soldiers, called Scutati, from their particular species of shield, were obliged to use iron greaves on their right legs." One of these may be seen in the monument of the gladiator Buto, in Montfaucon; and another in the Mosaic pavement at Bognor, in Surrey. <div eID="gen10166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10167" type="x-p"/> A target of brass between his shoulders - When not actually engaged, soldiers threw their shields behind their back, so that they appeared to rest or hang between the shoulders. <div eID="gen10167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10168" type="x-p"/> There are different opinions concerning this piece of armor, called here כידון kidon. Some think it was a covering for the shoulders; others, that it was a javelin or dart; others, that it was a lance; some, a club; and others, a sword. It is certainly distinguished from the shield, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.41">1Sam 17:41</reference>, and is translated a spear, <reference osisRef="Jos.8.18">Jos 8:18</reference>.
entries.15fdcb751e083a89c17324b391372048bf29addc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10169" type="x-p"/> The staff on his spear was like a weaver's beam - Either like that on which the warp is rolled, or that on which the cloth is rolled. We know not how thick this was, because there were several sorts of looms, and the sizes of the beams very dissimilar.
